s1.text: One input changes. Now your AI agent has to work out what that broke. Today, it has two options. Re-read everything. Accurate, but you pay for every token, every time. Or search for what looks related. Cheap, but blind to what matters.

s2.text: Agents build reports on their own earlier work, so every number quietly depends on inputs underneath. Correct one exchange rate, and some of those numbers are now wrong. But a total can depend on that rate without ever mentioning it. Similar words are not the same as real dependencies.

s3.text: ProofFlow is a context layer that follows structure instead of guessing. Every number keeps its receipts: exactly which inputs, and which tool, made it. So when something changes, the agent gets exactly what broke. Nothing more.

3a.text: ProofFlow is a context layer that follows structure instead of guessing.

3b.text: Every number keeps its receipts: exactly which inputs, and which tool, made it.

3c.text: So when something changes, the agent gets exactly what broke. Nothing more.

s4.text: An input, like the exchange rate, is saved as a version. A tool reads it, and leaves a receipt. The receipt points to its result, and each number in a report points to that result. Now, correct the rate. The change travels up those links. Both revenue figures are withheld, never shown stale. Support never read the rate, so it stays current, and is reused. Refresh re-runs only the affected steps.

s5.text: This is ProofFlow, live today. Upload orders as a CSV, preview them, and create two reports. Publish a corrected rate. Affected figures are withheld, and the graph shows exactly why. Refresh brings them current. A checked report can only be copied while every figure is current. Agents get the same workflow through MCP. Six tools, one download.

s6.text: Under the hood, it's small, and strict. At the center is the runtime. Every tool run produces an immutable result, and a receipt. Content goes into a store that verifies every hash. Relationships go into HydraDB, as a lineage graph. When a correction arrives, HydraDB walks that graph natively, to find everything downstream. That walk becomes the agent's context. Traverse the structure. Skip the re-read. The runtime re-runs stale steps in order, reuses what's current, and records new receipts. If evidence is missing, it fails closed. No fallback. No guess. Agents reach it through a browser app, a Python API, or an MCP server, choosing plans from typed tools, never arbitrary code.

s7.text: So how does it compare to today's approaches? We froze one study. Forty-eight real model calls, the same task for every method. Re-reading everything got all thirty-two reports right, for three dollars seventy-four. ProofFlow also got thirty-two of thirty-two, with a hundred forty-two thousand fewer input tokens, for a dollar thirty-eight. Sixty-three percent less. Vector search cost the same as ProofFlow, and got five right. Keyword search, twenty-five. Hybrid, twenty-eight. On a separate retail benchmark, thirty-eight of thirty-eight, with sixty-nine percent fewer evidence tokens. A plain dependency walk over the same links ties it. The win is recording the structure.
